steps.prompt: What is the difference between don’t have to and can’t?
options: Don’t have to = it isn’t necessary. Can’t = it isn’t allowed.
They both mean the same thing: that it is completely forbidden.
They both mean the same thing: that it is absolutely necessary.
steps.answer: Don’t have to = it isn’t necessary. Can’t = it isn’t allowed.
steps.why: This is the biggest trap in the topic: don’t have to is freedom, can’t and mustn’t are prohibition.

steps.title: must, have to, don’t have to, can
steps.html:
MeaningFormExample
it is necessarymust / have toYou have to arrive on time.
I feel it is importantmustYou must ask when you don’t understand.
it is not necessarydon’t have toYou don’t have to finish everything.
it is not allowedcan’t / mustn’tYou can’t say ‘I’m bad at this’.
it is allowedcanYou can say ‘I can’t do it yet’.
in the pasthad to / couldn’tWe had to knock. We couldn’t use phones.

Must and can take the base form and never change: he must, she can — no -s, no to.

Have to behaves like a normal verb: he has to, they don’t have to, did you have to?

Must usually comes from the speaker; have to usually comes from a rule outside. In everyday English have to is far more common.

Must has no past. Use had to: We had to knock, never we musted.

You met can for ability in the last lesson. Here it means permission — same word, different job.

steps.title: Recycled from Lesson 22: ability or obligation?
Before you read: one country has almost no school exams before the age of eighteen.
steps.sub: What do you think happened to its results? Decide first, then read and find out.

options.label: They are among the best in the world

steps.title: The country that took the rules away
steps.html:
In most school systems the rules are easy to see. You have to wear a uniform. You must be in your seat when the bell rings. You have to pass an entrance exam to get into a good school, and you have to sit tests every year to prove that you deserve your grade.

Finland decided to try something else. Finnish children do not start school until they are seven. They don’t have to take a single national exam until they are about eighteen. Nearly every child goes to a state school, and the few private schools that exist are not allowed to charge fees, so parents cannot buy a better education. Homework is light. The school day is short.

But one rule in Finland is very strict. To stand in front of a class, a teacher must have a master’s degree, and the courses that train them are harder to get into than law or medicine. A Finnish teacher doesn’t have to follow a national plan hour by hour — they can choose how to teach their own subject — because the system trusts a qualification it made difficult to get.

Its success surprised everybody. For twenty years Finland has been near the top of the international tests in reading, maths and science, with less testing than almost anyone else.

Nobody says the country is perfect, and its results have fallen a little since 2006. Copying it is not simple either: a system that trusts its teachers has to build that trust first, and that takes a generation. But the lesson is not that rules are bad. It is that a system has to decide where the rules belong — in the classroom, or in the choice of the person standing in it.

Sources. Finnish National Agency for Education, Education system · OECD PISA 2000–2022 country notes for Finland · Basic Education Act (Finland), on fees in private schools. Text written for this course.

steps.title: Read again for the details. Answer with a number or one word.
steps.html:
The country that took the rules away

In most school systems the rules are easy to see. You have to wear a uniform. You must be in your seat when the bell rings. You have to pass an entrance exam to get into a good school, and you have to sit tests every year to prove that you deserve your grade.

Finland decided to try something else. Finnish children do not start school until they are seven. They don’t have to take a single national exam until they are about eighteen. Nearly every child goes to a state school, and the few private schools that exist are not allowed to charge fees, so parents cannot buy a better education. Homework is light. The school day is short.

But one rule in Finland is very strict. To stand in front of a class, a teacher must have a master’s degree, and the courses that train them are harder to get into than law or medicine. A Finnish teacher doesn’t have to follow a national plan hour by hour — they can choose how to teach their own subject — because the system trusts a qualification it made difficult to get.

Its success surprised everybody. For twenty years Finland has been near the top of the international tests in reading, maths and science, with less testing than almost anyone else.

Nobody says the country is perfect, and its results have fallen a little since 2006. Copying it is not simple either: a system that trusts its teachers has to build that trust first, and that takes a generation. But the lesson is not that rules are bad. It is that a system has to decide where the rules belong — in the classroom, or in the choice of the person standing in it.

Sources. Finnish National Agency for Education, Education system · OECD PISA 2000–2022 country notes for Finland · Basic Education Act (Finland), on fees in private schools. Text written for this course.

steps.title: Write the rules of a place you know: your school, your workplace or your home.
steps.sub: Six rules. Use a different form in each one.
steps.html:
1. Plan: something necessary → something you feel is important → something optional → something forbidden → something allowed → one rule from the past.
  • You have to …
  • You must …
  • You don’t have to …
  • You can’t …
  • You can …
  • When I was at school we had to …
You have toYou mustYou don’t have toYou can’tYou mustn’tYou canwe had towe couldn’tstrictgradeentrance examqualification
steps.modelHtml:
• I wrote six rules.
  • One uses have to and one uses must.
  • One uses don’t have to for something optional.
  • One uses can’t or mustn’t for something forbidden.
  • One is in the past with had to or couldn’t.
